text: Patricia Jane Berg (February 13, 1918 – September 10, 2006) was an American professional golfer and a founding member and the first president of the LPGA. She holds the all-time record for most major wins by a female golfer with 15 major title wins, which remains unmatched. She is a member of the World Golf Hall of Fame. In winter, she was also a speed skater. Born in Minneapolis, Minnesota, Berg expressed an early interest in football and played quarterback on a local team that included future Oklahoma Sooners head coach Bud Wilkinson. At age 13, she began golf in 1931 at her parents' suggestion; by 1934, she won the Minneapolis City Championship and the following year claimed a state amateur title. She attended the University of Minnesota and was a member of Kappa Kappa Gamma sorority. She gained national attention by reaching the final of the 1935 U.S. Women's Amateur, losing to Glenna Collett-Vare in Vare's final Amateur victory. Berg won the Titleholders in 1937. In 1938, she won the U.S. Women's Amateur at Westmoreland and the Women's Western Amateur. With a victory in the 1938 Titleholders Championship and a spot on the winning Curtis Cup team, she was selected as the Associated Press Woman Athlete of the Year, the first of three times she earned the honor. In 1939, she won her third consecutive Titleholders, though she missed the U.S. Women's Amateur due to an appendix operation. After winning 29 amateur titles, she turned professional in 1940. Her career was interrupted by an automobile accident in December 1941, during a trip to a fund-raising event with Helen Dettweiler, which shattered her knee. She recovered, volunteered for the United States Marine Corps, and was commissioned a second lieutenant in 1942, serving in the Marine Reserves from 1942 to 1945. Despite concerns about ending her golf career, Berg returned in 1943 after a locker room fall broke adhesions in her leg and won the Women's Western Open. She won the inaugural U.S. Women's Open in 1946. In 1948, she helped establish the forerunner of the LPGA, the Women's Professional Golf Association (WPGA), winning three tournaments that season and in 1949. When the LPGA was officially founded in 1950, Berg was one of the 13 founding members and served as its first president. She won a total of 57 events on the LPGA and WPGA circuit, was runner-up in the 1957 Open at Winged Foot, and in the 1956 and 1959 LPGA Championships. She won the 1953, 1957, and 1958 Women's Western Opens, the 1955 and 1957 Titleholders, both considered majors at the time, and her last victory came in 1962. She was voted the Associated Press Woman Athlete of the Year in 1942, 1955, and 1938. From 1953 to 1956, she won the Vare Trophy three times for having the lowest scoring average on the LPGA. She was the LPGA Tour's top money winner twice, in 1954 and 1957, and holds the all-time record for seven Titleholders wins. Her 15 women's major golf championships include the seven Titleholders victories, seven Women's Western Open wins, and the 1946 U.S. Women's Open championship. In 1959, Berg became the first woman to hit a hole-in-one during a USGA competition at the U.S. Women's Open. In 1963, she received the Bob Jones Award, the highest honor from the United States Golf Association for distinguished sportsmanship in golf. She received the 1986 Old Tom Morris Award from the Golf Course Superintendents Association of America, the organization's highest honor. The LPGA established the Patty Berg Award in 1978. In her later years, she teamed with PGA Tour player and fellow Fort Myers, Florida resident Nolan Henke to establish the Nolan Henke/Patty Berg Junior Masters to promote young players. Berg was sponsored on the LPGA Tour her entire career by Joe Jemsek, owner of Cog Hill Golf & Country Club in Lemont, Illinois, the site of the PGA Tour's Western Open from 1991 to 2006, and represented St. Andrews Golf & Country Club in West Chicago, Illinois, on the women's circuit for over 60 years. She told Chicagoland Golf magazine she taught over 16,000 clinics in her lifetime, many sponsored by Chicago-based Wilson Sporting Goods and known as "The Patty Berg Hit Parade," and estimated that she personally introduced over half a million new players to golf. She was a member of Wilson's Advisory Staff for 66 years until her death. In December 2004, she announced she had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and died in Fort Myers from complications of the disease 21 months later at the age of 88.
